title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
authors: John A. Dove; Noah J. Trudeau
affiliations: School of Creative Enterprise and Market Systems, Sorrell College of Business Troy University Troy Alabama USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. Using interrupted time series analysis with and without control, we find that the passage of the Pendleton Act did, in fact, result in lower borrowing costs for the federal government of between 63 and 84 basis points depending on specification. Implications are discussed.

title: Supplemental Material for Revisiting the Assumption of a Self-Regulatory Loop: A Cross-Lagged Study of the Relationship Between Role Ambiguity and Feedback Seeking
Deep Tangency Portfolio
authors: Guanhao Feng; Liang Jiang; Junye Li; Yizhi Song; Yuanzhi Wang
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon 999077, Hong Kong SAR; International School of Finance, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; International Business School, Hainan University, Haikou 570228, China; University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China
abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: G. title: Learning from a Biased Sample
authors: Roshni Sahoo; Lihua Lei; Stefan Wager
affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University, New York 10027; Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, Palo Alto, California 94305
abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. RS is further supported by a NSF GRFP under grant DGE-1656518, a Stanford Data Science PhD Fellowship, and a Stanford Diversifying Academia Recruiting Excellence (DARE) Fellowship. title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
authors: Chen Chen; Pengyu Qian; Jingwei Zhang
affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; School of Data Science, School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518172, China
abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. Zhang is partly supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) [Grant 72394361] and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Mathematical Foundations for Artificial Intelligence [2023B1212010001]. title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
authors: Lin Nan; Lin Qiu; Xiaoyan Wen; Ronghuo Zheng
affiliations: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas 76129; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
authors: Diego Aparicio; Duncan I. Simester
affiliations: Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; MIT Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142
abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
authors: Zhongbin Wang; Shiliang Cui; Yongjian Li; Qian Zhang
affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; Business School, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China; School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China
abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Zhang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 724B2024]. title: Short-horizon capital in a bank-centered financial system: Japanese mutual fund launches relative to the U.S.
authors: Toshiki Honda; Alan Guoming Huang; Daisuke Miyakawa; Sho Nishiuchi; Russ Wermers
abstract: Abstract The median time from launch to peak assets under management (AUM) is nine months for Japanese active domestic equity mutual funds, versus 4.6 years for comparable U.S. funds. Japanese funds also grow much less from launch to peak, as strong initial inflows quickly give way to persistent outflows, while U.S. funds continue to attract net inflows for years. We link this compressed life cycle to Japan’s bank-centered, concentrated distribution system and front-loaded sales compensation. A larger launch size and higher sales load each predict earlier peak AUM in Japan, but not in the U.S.; within Japan, stronger distribution networks are associated with larger launches and earlier peaks, while longer pre-inception sales periods are associated with larger launch sizes and higher sales loads. The evidence shows that the same market-based financial product can follow different life cycles when embedded in different national systems of intermediation and compensation. Japan’s prolonged weak equity-market environment provides an additional context in which investors may reassess newly launched funds as realized performance becomes observable. Our findings suggest that incentives rewarding initial sales can mobilize capital rapidly without generating durable asset retention in an institutional environment such as Japan’s.

title: Adapting to the new abnormal: multinational corporations’ foreign subsidiary investment and country resilience to climate change
authors: Chang Hoon Oh; Jorge Rivera; Jennifer Oetzel
abstract: Abstract As climate change (CC) increasingly disrupts infrastructure, supply chains, labor availability, and public services, multinational corporations (MNCs) face growing uncertainty when selecting locations for foreign expansion. We examine whether host-country CC resilience has become an important determinant of international investment and how firm capabilities shape this relationship. Drawing on socio-ecological resilience theory and the resilience and turbulence framework, we analyze Global Fortune 500 firms investing across 155 countries between 2003 and 2017. We find that MNCs establish more wholly owned subsidiaries in countries with higher CC resilience, indicating that resilience is emerging as a strategic location-specific advantage. This relationship is stronger for firms with well-developed ESG capabilities and prior experience operating in resilient countries, but weaker for firms with greater financial slack. Our findings suggest that managers should incorporate CC resilience into location decisions alongside traditional economic and institutional criteria while considering their firms’ resource and capability profile to assess how effectively they can leverage host-country CC resilience. For policymakers, the results indicate that strengthening CC resilience can improve not only adaptation to CC but also national competitiveness in attracting MNC foreign direct investment. Overall, CC resilience is becoming a strategic determinant of where MNCs choose to invest.

title: Interrogating youth drinking declines: Youth transitions, delayed onset and the changing frequency of drinking amongst young people in the United Kingdom
authors: Emily Nicholls; Muhammad Waqas
affiliations: University of York, UK; University of Bradford, UK
abstract: As transitions to adulthood become increasingly delayed and precarious across high-income countries, youth drinking has notably declined. This paper interrogates the ‘delayed onset’ theory, investigating whether – despite the ‘decline’ – individual consumption increases as young people age (meaning their alcohol consumption may eventually ‘catch up’ with that of previous cohorts). Analysing UK Household Longitudinal Study data over a decade, we examine trends in consumption frequency and Heavy Episodic Drinking. Findings demonstrate that both metrics increase as individuals age, with higher consumption associated with male gender and increased education / household income. Findings are considered through a sociological lens attendant to the precarity, unevenness and protractedness of youth transitions and the entanglements of gender, class and drinking, building on cross-sectional studies to help develop an evidence base around ‘delayed onset’. This has implications for how drinking declines are conceptualised and for broader sociological understandings of contemporary youth transitions to adulthood.

title: Educational gradients of housework and childcare time in East Asian and Anglophone countries from the 1980s to the 2020s
authors: Matthew Henglong Luo; Grace Chang; Man-Yee Kan
affiliations: University of Oxford, UK
abstract: The past half-century witnessed substantial changes in both behaviours and ideologies concerning the division of labour and child-rearing. This study aims to examine how educational attainment is associated with housework and childcare time for both men and women, how these patterns have evolved from the 1980s to the 2020s, and whether the evolution differs between East Asian and Anglophone countries. Using time-diary data from two East Asian countries (Japan and South Korea) and three Anglophone countries (the USA, the UK, and Canada), our analyses reveal that (a) education promotes gender convergence in housework contributions; (b) higher-educated parents generally spend more time on childcare; (c) educational gaps in housework are relatively stable over time, while educational gaps in childcare increase over time; (d) the trends differ between East Asian and Anglophone countries in terms of the evolution stage. These findings are discussed regarding the implications for gender revolution and intergenerational stratification.

title: Visualizing Uncertainty in Dispersion Forecasting: Effects on User Perceptions and Communication
authors: Helen Miller; Susan Leadbetter; Sarah C. Jenkins
affiliations: Met Office Exeter UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Operational dispersion forecasts have traditionally been produced deterministically, producing a single best estimate of the situation despite inherent uncertainty. Recently, there has been a paradigmatic shift toward providing uncertainty information as part of operational aviation forecasts. Yet, little is currently known about how exactly this information should be presented or about its effects on understanding and perceptions (vs. purely deterministic information). Using an ensemble of dispersion forecasts (produced using varying inputs) allows visualization of some of the dispersion uncertainty. Here, we compared how deterministic versus ensemble visualizations affected the graphical and written guidance provided. Across two scenarios featuring volcanic eruptions, 30 participants working in atmospheric dispersion were asked to produce an advisory graphic (a polygon encompassing an area of volcanic ash) and a written statement, as well as to rate the visualizations for utility, clarity, and importance. Overall, we find that participants drew bigger polygons (encompassing a larger geographical extent) in the uncertain, ensemble condition, though these were more consistent than those in the deterministic condition. Advisory statements in the ensemble condition also reflected greater uncertainty. Broadly, perceptions of the uncertainty information were neutral to positive, though graphics where less ash was shown were perceived as less useful. Our findings indicate that the presence of uncertainty information can influence communication products generated, underlining the importance of testing ensemble visualizations with users.

title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
authors: Zuzana Murdoch; Benny Geys
affiliations: Department of Government University of Bergen Bergen Norway; Department of Economics BI Norwegian Business School Bergen Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. We also uncover that leaks become less—not more—likely when there is a negative expert assessment of a policy proposal (relative to a control group receiving no expert assessment). Our findings help elucidate the information‐sharing dilemmas faced by public administrators.

title: Correction
Small N, High Stakes: Simulating Adverse Impact With Bayesian Logistic Regression Analysis and Permutation Tests
authors: Patrick J. Rolwes; Karyssa A. Courey; Frederick L. Oswald; Michelle P. Martín-Raugh
affiliations: The University of Texas at Arlington; Louisiana State University; University of California
abstract: Organizations frequently evaluate adverse impact with rules of thumb and statistical tests that perform poorly when hiring cohorts are small, raising scientific concerns that have legal and ethical implications. To address these concerns, this study conducts Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests as two new approaches to conducting adverse impact analysis under small-sample conditions. Simulations were varied across a realistic range of effect sizes, selection rates, and group sample sizes. The performance of each method was evaluated in terms of Type I error rates and statistical power. Results indicated that both Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests are viable alternatives to traditional methods under small-sample conditions. Bayesian odds-ratio rules with noninformative or weakly informative priors in particular demonstrated higher power than frequentist methods at small sample sizes, although no method reached .80 power on average. Their Type I error rates sometimes exceeded the nominal .05 level but remained well below those of the 4/5ths rule. Implications and advantages of each method are discussed in detail.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Consumer Fairness Seeking in Live-Stream E-Commerce
authors: Baozhuang Niu; Jianhua Zhang; Qiyang Li; Xinhu Yu; Yulan Wang
abstract: As live-stream e-commerce rapidly expands and gains popularity among consumers, many brand owners have supplemented their self-owned direct-selling channels with live-stream selling channels to utilize social network effects of key opinion leaders (KOLs). This dual-channel structure creates price discrepancy issues, prompting consumers to raise concerns about price fairness. Therefore, brand owners are motivated to coordinate pricing strategies, balancing cooperation and competition across channels. We build a game-theoretical model to investigate how consumers' peer-induced fairness seeking influences the price decisions of a brand owner (in the direct-selling channel) and the KOL (in the live-stream selling channel). Interestingly, we find that consumers' increased fairness concerns may paradoxically lead to increased prices in both channels, challenging the conventional expectation of price-cutting competition. We further demonstrate that consumers' fairness seeking may either benefit or harm both sellers, depending on the strength of network effects and various factors related to competition intensity. The non-monotonic impacts of consumer fairness seeking are driven by the brand owner's dueling strategic incentives to secure (or relinquish) its direct-selling business to compete with (or favor) the live-stream selling under different situations. Finally, we identify “win-win”, “lose-lose”, and “lose-win” outcomes that consumer fairness seeking can cause for the brand owner and KOL.

title: EXPRESS: Supercharging the Confidence Trap: Too-Big-to-Fail and Man-Made Disasters
authors: Akhil Bhardwaj; Henk Akkermans; Luk N. Van Wassenhove
abstract: Man-made disasters are always shocking, especially when they involve loss of life. The shock is even greater when such disasters are attributed to failures in highly regulated organizations like Boeing, long known for engineering excellence and safety. In the spirit of pragmatic inquiry that considers attenuating the likelihood of disasters an urgent and important problem, we explore the underlying dynamics that can lead to such outcomes. We draw on an agent-based modelling approach within a system dynamics framework. We argue that operational and organizational complexity creates barriers to identifying failures that contribute to disasters. A key contributor to this dynamic is the weakening of regulatory oversight, as both regulators and operators fall into a “confidence trap” – a mistaken belief that past risk-taking success justifies continued risk-taking. This dynamic is exacerbated when the organization in question is perceived as “too big to fail,” which shields it from market selection mechanisms. To mitigate these factors, we propose two policy levers. First, we propose financial clawbacks that require executives to return part of their compensation in the event of a disaster. This aligns incentives of the regulator and executives by injecting the latter’s “skin in the game,” and attenuates the moral hazard problem. Second, we propose third-party monitoring and auditing that serve to mitigate regulatory oversight and better utilize expertise. Simulations indicate these levers significantly reduce the likelihood and impact of failures that lead to disasters, offering a robust logic of pursuit.

title: The Reversal of the Gender Gap in Automation: Evidence From the US Labor Market
authors: Montserrat Martí; Alejandro Micco; Francisca Pérez
affiliations: Department of Economics Brown University Providence Rhode Island USA; Faculty of Economics and Business University of Chile Santiago Chile; Business School Adolfo Ibáñez University Santiago Chile
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper documents a reversal in the US gender gap in the probability of automation, 1976–2019. Women initially had higher automation probabilities than men, but the gap narrowed and reversed. The aggregate change occurs mainly within sectors, from clerical and retail sales to professional and technical occupations. The reversal is associated with education and occupational work‐hour structure. It is concentrated among newer cohorts: cohort‐specific gaps absorb most of the trend and attenuate as education, work‐hour structure, and social skills are added. These patterns are consistent with broad changes in women's occupational conditions but do not identify their causal mechanisms.
journal: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: Beyond Union Membership: Wage Formation and Collective Institutions
authors: Fredrik B. Kostøl; Elin W. Svarstad
affiliations: Department of Industrial Economics and Technology Management Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) Trondheim Norway; Fafo Institute of Labour and Social Research Oslo Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Using linked Norwegian employer‐employee register data for 2016–2023, we examine how union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage relate to wages. Union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage represent distinct dimensions of collective presence and should not be treated as conceptually equivalent. We find that union members earn more than non‐members irrespective of coverage, while the relationship between wages and union density depends on membership and coverage. Collective agreements are not associated with a uniform wage premium. However, covered firms have smaller white‐collar wage premia and a weaker relationship between wages and productivity for white‐collar workers.

title: How Do Employees Navigate Destructive Leadership Behaviour? A Focus on SMEs
authors: Afsaneh Bagheri; Safoora Pitsi; Gholamreza Polooee
affiliations: Lincoln International Business School University of Lincoln Lincoln LN6 7TS UK; Excelsia University College Pennant Hills NSW 2120 Australia; University of Wollongong Wollongong NSW 2500 Australia; Faculty of Entrepreneurship University of Tehran Tehran Iran
abstract: Abstract Destructive leadership has detrimental effects on employee and organizational performance, yet we know little about how employees respond to such leadership behaviour, particularly in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs), where close interpersonal relationships and limited organizational support constrain employees’ responses. Drawing on Leader‐Member Exchange (LMX) theory, we examine the coping strategies employees adopt to navigate destructive leadership behaviour and the mechanisms that shape these strategies. We conducted 26 semi‐structured interviews with employees across diverse SMEs and job roles and analysed the data thematically. We identify three coping strategies: (i) adaptation, (ii) resistance and (iii) exit. Employees’ choice among these strategies depends on their assessment of their tolerance of personal and professional risks and their perceived power to influence or change their situation. These evaluations determine whether employees accommodate their leaders’ destructive behaviour, resist it or disengage entirely by leaving the organization. Our findings extend LMX theory by highlighting employees’ active role in evaluating their interactions and adapting their responses according to the associated risks and their power to influence or change their situation. The study also highlights the contextual dynamics of SMEs and offers insights for organizations seeking to recognize the effects of destructive leadership and support employees.

title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
authors: Jamie Coen; Patrick Coen; Anne-Caroline Hüser
affiliations: Imperial College London , U.K; Warwick Business School , U.K; Bank of England , U.K
abstract: Abstract Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.

title: Hedging by Giving: Spiritual Insurance and Religious Donations
authors: Yu-Jane Liu; Juanjuan Meng; Dalin Sheng; Guangxin Yang; Yu Zhang
affiliations: Peking University Guanghua School of Management; Southwestern University of Finance and Economics China Center for Behavioral Economics and Finance; Xiamen University School of Management
abstract: Abstract We investigate “spiritual insurance”—a mental strategy for coping with risk, where individuals engage in good deeds, including donations, in exchange for perceived blessings and protection. Using bank transactional data, we show that higher income uncertainty and health shocks lead to increased donations, particularly to religious charities. Moreover, individuals who donate to religious charities tend to reduce insurance expenditures. In a field experiment on millions of potential donors through an online platform, we find that spiritual insurance narratives increase giving, providing direct causal evidence for such a motive. Our findings provide new evidence on how spiritual insurance affects household risk-coping behavior.
